summary: Describes how to break Sun's CellB video encoding into packets for transport over RTP. It is aimed at implementors of video applications that want to use RTP with CellB.

eli5.summary: A video is cut into little packets with labels so that it can travel across the network and be put back together.

questions: how to send cellb video over rtp
how is cellb video sent over rtp
what is the cellb rtp header
what is a cellb skip code
subtitle: How to chop Sun's CellB video stream into RTP packets that survive packet loss.

tldr.problem: Sun's CellB video encoding produces a bytestream of codes for 4x4 pixel blocks, and applications needed a standard way to carry it in RTP packets over a lossy network.
tldr.mechanism: Each RTP packet gets an extra 8-byte CellB header giving the position of its first cell and the frame width and height, so a receiver can place the cells even if earlier packets were lost.
tldr.outcome: Implementors of RTP video applications can send CellB video interoperably, and Sun states that CellB is available for use without any license.

today: RFC 2029 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines the packetization of CellB over RTP, which builds on RFC 1889.

sections.title: What CellB Is
sections.content:
RFC 2029 describes a packetization scheme for the CellB video encoding from Sun Microsystems. It is meant for implementors of video applications that want to use RTP and CellB.

The Cell image compression algorithm is a variable bit-rate video coding scheme. It aims at high quality and low bit-rate at low computational cost. There are two versions, CellA and CellB. CellA is designed for stored video shown locally and is not covered. CellB is derived from CellA and optimized for network-based video. It is computationally symmetric, so encoding and decoding cost about the same. It uses a fixed colormap and vector quantization in the YUV color space.
sections.eli5: CellB is a way of squeezing video so it is small enough to send over a network. This document explains how to put that squeezed video into packets.

sections.title: How RTP Is Used
sections.content: The RTP timestamp for CellB is in units of 90KHz. All packets that carry parts of the same frame use the same timestamp value. The RTP marker bit marks the end of a frame, so a receiver knows when a frame is complete.
sections.eli5: Every packet from the same picture gets the same time label. The last packet of a picture gets a special flag that says it is the end.

sections.title: The CellB Header
sections.content:
To make the packet stream robust to packet loss, an extra header is added to each RTP packet. It identifies where the first cell of the packet sits within the current frame. It also carries the width and height of the frame in pixels. The size can only change between frames, but it is sent in every packet to keep the encoding simple.

The header has four fields, Cell X Location, Cell Y Location, Width of Image and Height of Image. All are 16-bit unsigned integers in network byte order, placed at the start of each RTP payload, followed by the compressed CellB data.

The location fields are in cell coordinates, not pixel coordinates. Cells are 4x4 blocks of pixels, so each cell coordinate ranges from 0 up to 1/4 of the same dimension in pixels.
sections.eli5: Each packet starts with a note saying which tile of the picture comes first and how big the whole picture is. Then a packet that arrives alone still knows where it belongs.

sections.title: Packetization Rules
sections.content:
A packet can be any size the implementor chooses, up to a full frame. The one hard rule is that all multi-byte codes must be completely contained within a single packet, so a code is never split across two packets.

As a general guideline, the implementor should avoid packet sizes that cause fragmentation by the network.
sections.eli5: You can put as many tiles in a packet as you like, but you must never cut one tile's instructions in half between two packets.

sections.title: The CellB Byte Stream
sections.content:
The appendix describes the stream inside the packets. It consists of cell codes, skip codes and quantization-table codes.

A cell code is 4 bytes and describes one 4x4 pixel cell. The first two bytes are a bitmask with one bit per pixel. A set bit means the pixel uses luminance Y(1), and a clear bit means Y(0). The bitmask is normalized so its most significant bit is always 0. The next byte is a U/V code, an index into a table of chrominance vectors. The last byte is a Y/Y code, an index into a table of two-component luminance vectors. Deriving these tables is outside the scope of the memo.

A one-byte skip code tells the decoder to skip the next S+1 cells in the frame, and at most 32 cells can be skipped.

Two one-byte codes announce a new quantization table: 11111110 for a new Y/Y table and 11111111 for a new U/V table. Each is followed by 512 bytes of table data. The sample encoder and decoder do not implement these, though future CellB codecs may.
sections.eli5: Each tile is described by a small code: which pixels are light or dark and which colour to use. There is also a shortcut code that says to skip tiles that did not change.

sections.title: Availability and Status
sections.content: Appendix B records the view of Sun Microsystems that CellB is publicly available for use without any license. The RFC is a Standards Track document, and its metadata lists it as a Proposed Standard.
sections.eli5: The company that made CellB says anyone can use it for free.

fields.name: Cell X Location
fields.desc: Column of the first cell in this packet, in cell coordinates.

fields.name: Cell Y Location
fields.desc: Row of the first cell in this packet, in cell coordinates.

fields.name: Bitmask
fields.desc: Which pixels of the 4x4 cell use Y(1) rather than Y(0).

fields.name: U/V Code
fields.desc: Index into the chrominance vector table.

fields.name: Y/Y Code
fields.desc: Index into the luminance vector table.
